pages.content:
# Context discovery

## Purpose

Before an agent edits a repository, it needs to find what's stable and true about it — build/test commands, conventions, architecture boundaries, domain rules — without guessing or relying on a human to explain it live. Context discovery is the capability that lets an agent locate that information on its own.

## Desired outcomes

- An agent new to the repository can find its entry point for "how do I work here" without being told where to look.
- That entry point stays current with the repository (not a stale onboarding doc from a year ago).
- The agent finds only what's relevant to its current task, not an undifferentiated pile (see [progressive disclosure](../principles/progressive-disclosure.md)).

## Maturity model

- **Level 0 — Implicit**: Project rules live only in people's heads, chat history, or scattered PR comments. No file an agent would read on its own states them.
- **Level 1 — Discoverable**: A root-level file (README, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or equivalent) exists and states the basics, but may be incomplete or drift out of date.
- **Level 2 — Usable**: The entry-point file accurately covers build, test, and key conventions; an agent can act on it directly without trial and error.
- **Level 3 — Integrated**: Discovery is scoped — nested/linked instructions for subprojects, links to architecture and domain docs — so an agent loads only what its current task needs.
- **Level 4 — Adaptive**: Gaps found during real work (an agent hits an undocumented constraint) feed back into updating the entry-point docs, closing the loop.

## Repository signals

- Presence of `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.cursor/rules/`, `GEMINI.md`, or a clearly agent-facing README section.
- Whether the documented build/test commands actually run successfully (verify — don't infer from the file existing; see the [verification](verification.md) concept and the evidence rule in ../system/governance.md).
- Whether the file is scoped (links out to deeper docs) or a monolith.
- Git history: does the entry-point file get updated alongside structural changes, or has it visibly rotted?

## Possible improvements

- Add a minimal entry-point file stating how to build, test, and where deeper docs live — see the [documented repository entry points](../practices/documented-repository-entry-points.md) practice.
- Split an overgrown single file into a root summary plus linked, scoped pages.
- Verify and fix stale commands in an existing entry-point file.

## Validation methods

- Actually run the documented build/test commands in a clean checkout; note any that fail or are missing.
- Ask an agent unfamiliar with the repo to complete a small real task using only the discoverable context; note what it had to guess.

## Failure modes

- An entry-point file exists but is stale or wrong, which is worse than none (false confidence).
- The file is copied across harnesses by hand and drifts out of sync (see ../mappings/harnesses/persistent-instructions.md for how this brain avoids that).
- Everything relevant is dumped into one huge file, defeating progressive disclosure.

## Related concepts

- [Verification](verification.md) — discoverability without correctness is misleading
- Architecture awareness — often the deeper content a scoped entry point links to

## Harness mappings

- Context discovery in coding-agent harnesses

## Evidence

This brain's own ingest playbook and the AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/copilot-instructions.md triad it maintains is a live example of level 3 (scoped, harness-mapped, single-sourced via APM). See the dogfooding assessment at ../assessments/brain/2026-07-15.md for a concrete maturity rating against this model.
pages.title: Context discovery

pages.content:
# Feedback loops

## Purpose

Without a feedback loop, the same gap in instructions or tooling gets rediscovered — and re-explained by a human — every time an agent hits it. Feedback loops are the capability that turns an observed failure or correction into a durable improvement, so the repository (or this brain) gets measurably better over repeated use instead of staying static.

## Desired outcomes

- A recurring correction a human gives an agent gets written down somewhere agents will see next time, not just repeated verbally each session.
- Validation failures (see [verification](verification.md)) are visible and traceable back to their cause.
- There's a lightweight, habitual place to record "this didn't work" outcomes — not just successes.

## Maturity model

- **Level 0 — Implicit**: Corrections and failures are handled live and forgotten; no record exists.
- **Level 1 — Discoverable**: Some mechanism exists to record outcomes (an issues log, a changelog, this brain's own log.md pattern) even if inconsistently used.
- **Level 2 — Usable**: Recorded outcomes are specific and findable enough that a future agent (or human) can act on them without re-deriving the lesson.
- **Level 3 — Integrated**: Recorded outcomes are actually reflected back into instructions, tooling, or playbooks — not just logged and ignored.
- **Level 4 — Adaptive**: The loop runs without prompting — an agent (per governance rules) proposes the instruction/tooling update itself when it notices a recurring gap, subject to review for anything beyond a single-repo fix.

## Repository signals

- Existence of any changelog, retro notes, or "lessons learned" file, and whether entries are specific enough to act on.
- Whether repeated correction patterns show up in PR review comments without ever being written into instructions.
- Whether CI/test failures are just re-run until green, or actually investigated and fed back into fixes/docs.

## Possible improvements

- Add a lightweight log for recording outcomes if none exists (level 0 → 1) — this brain's own log.md is a working example.
- Make an existing log specific enough to be actionable rather than vague ("fixed some issues") (level 1 → 2).
- Add a habit (playbook step, PR checklist item) that asks "does this outcome suggest an instruction or tooling update?" (level 2 → 3/4).

## Validation methods

- Sample recent recorded outcomes and check whether a future reader could act on them without additional context.
- Check whether a known recent failure or correction is reflected anywhere in current instructions.

## Failure modes

- A log exists but nothing ever reads it — write-only feedback isn't a loop.
- Outcomes are recorded too vaguely to act on ("improved things") — see the evidence rule in ../system/governance.md.
- Feedback closes the loop for one repository but never generalizes, so the same gap recurs elsewhere (this is exactly what the continuous-agent-readiness-improvement playbook's step 13 and the playbook-improvement page type exist to fix, carefully and only with review).

## Related concepts

- [Verification](verification.md) — validation failures are one of the most concrete feedback signals available
- Durable memory — the persistence layer feedback loops write their outcomes into

## Harness mappings

- (none yet — feedback loops are realized through repository conventions, not harness-specific tooling)

## Evidence

This brain's own `log.md` (append-only, newest first, required by ../system/conventions.md) is a working level-1/2 example of this concept applied to the brain itself; the experiments and playbook-improvement page types exist specifically to push this toward level 3/4 for repository-improvement knowledge.
pages.title: Feedback loops

pages.content:
# Verification

## Purpose

An agent that can't validate its own change is forced to either guess it's correct or hand every change to a human to check. Verification is the capability that lets an agent (or a human) confirm a change did what it was supposed to, ideally with the smallest check that gives a confident answer.

## Desired outcomes

- An agent can run a check after making a change and get a trustworthy pass/fail signal.
- The agent can pick a targeted check for the kind of change it made, instead of always running the full suite (or nothing).
- Failures point at what broke clearly enough to act on, not just "something is wrong."

## Maturity model

- **Level 0 — Implicit**: Validation is manual and undocumented — someone runs something, but it's not written down anywhere an agent could find.
- **Level 1 — Discoverable**: Build and test commands are documented (e.g. in the entry-point file from [context discovery](context-discovery.md)).
- **Level 2 — Usable**: Agents can choose a targeted check based on the kind of change made (e.g. "backend change → run backend unit tests," not always the full suite).
- **Level 3 — Integrated**: Validation is automated, observable, and reliable — CI runs it, results are visible, and it isn't flaky enough to be ignored.
- **Level 4 — Adaptive**: Validation failures feed back into future instructions or playbooks (e.g. a recurring failure mode gets documented so agents avoid it next time).

## Repository signals

- Documented build/test commands exist — and actually work when run (verify, don't infer from a README claim).
- Whether tests are organized so a subset can be run for a given change type (unit vs. integration vs. e2e, per-package test targets).
- CI configuration: does it run on every change, and is the result visible/actionable?
- History of flaky or ignored CI — a signal that "integrated" is superficial.

## Possible improvements

- Document the full test command if missing (level 0 → 1).
- Add a change-type-to-command mapping so agents don't default to the slowest possible check (level 1 → 2) — this is the kind of practice recorded under ../practices/README.md.
- Fix flaky or silently-skipped CI so "integrated" is actually trustworthy (level 2 → 3).

## Validation methods

- Run the documented commands from a clean checkout and confirm they pass/fail as expected.
- Introduce a deliberate small bug and confirm the documented checks catch it.
- Check CI history for flakiness or checks that are effectively always green regardless of correctness.

## Failure modes

- Tests exist but are so slow that agents (and humans) skip them, defaulting back to level 0 in practice.
- A documented command is stale and silently no-ops instead of failing loudly.
- "Full test suite always" as the only option pushes agents toward broad, slow validation instead of targeted, fast validation — a level-1-pretending-to-be-level-2 trap.

## Related concepts

- [Context discovery](context-discovery.md) — where the validation commands are documented
- [Feedback loops](feedback-loops.md) — verification is the fastest, most concrete feedback loop a repository can offer

## Harness mappings

- (none yet — verification is largely harness-neutral; a stack-specific mapping, e.g. `pytest` vs. `cargo test` selection commands, belongs under ../mappings/tools/ once recorded)

## Evidence

Used as the founding spec's own worked example (section 3.1); this brain's dogfooding assessment (../assessments/brain/2026-07-15.md) rates this repository's own verification maturity and motivates the validate-brain.py script as a level 1→2 move.

pages.content:
# Documented repository entry points

## Problem

Agents (and new contributors) working in a repository with no discoverable entry point have to reverse-engineer how to build, test, and where key documentation lives — from README fragments, CI config, or trial and error. This directly limits [context discovery](../concepts/context-discovery.md) at level 0, and indirectly blocks [verification](../concepts/verification.md) if build/test commands aren't findable.

## Proposed practice

Add one short root-level file (or a root file plus a small number of clearly linked, scoped files for larger repos) that states, and only states:

- how to build the project,
- how to run tests (and, if applicable, how to run a targeted subset),
- where architecture documentation lives (if any),
- where domain/business-rule documentation lives (if any),
- how to find more detail for anything not covered here.

It is explicitly not a place to restate everything about the repository — it points, it doesn't duplicate (see [progressive disclosure](../principles/progressive-disclosure.md)).

## Expected benefit

**High.** This is usually the single highest-leverage, lowest-cost first step for a repository at context-discovery level 0 — it unblocks nearly every other agent-readiness concept, since an agent that can't build or test the project can't productively do much else.

## Applicable scope

- Repositories with no existing agent-facing entry-point file (no README section, no AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/copilot-instructions.md/equivalent).
- Repositories with a single primary stack, or where a short root file can reasonably summarize a small number of stacks.

## Non-applicable scope

- Repositories that already have an accurate, current entry-point file — the improvement there is usually verifying/fixing it, not adding a new one (a different, narrower practice).
- Very large monorepos where a single root file can't meaningfully summarize dozens of unrelated subprojects — those need a root file plus scoped per-subproject files, not covered by this practice's current scope.

## Implementation options

- A dedicated `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` (harness-specific realizations — see ../mappings/harnesses/persistent-instructions.md).
- A clearly labeled section in an existing `README.md` (lower cost, works for harnesses without a dedicated convention, at some cost to progressive disclosure if the README is already long).
- A generic `docs/agent-context.md` linked from the README, for repos that want one file usable regardless of harness.

## Cost

**Low.** Writing an accurate root entry-point file for a repository with a single stack typically takes under an hour once the actual build/test commands are verified. Ongoing cost is keeping it current — cheap if it's short, more expensive if it accumulates unrelated content over time.

## Risks

- The file can go stale if not updated alongside build/test changes, producing false confidence (worse than no file — see [context discovery](../concepts/context-discovery.md)'s failure modes).
- If not kept short, it tends to accumulate unrelated content over time, undermining progressive disclosure.

## Rollback

Trivial: delete the file (or the README section), or revert the commit. No other system depends on it.

## Evidence

Applied to this brain's own repository as the first recorded experiment — see ../experiments/brain/2026-07-15-entry-points-practice.md. One data point: `experimental`, not yet `recommended` (per ../system/governance.md's promotion criteria, that needs more than one context). This brain's own AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md-equivalent setup (the ingest-playbook trigger files) is a related but distinct case — it documents a workflow, not build/test/architecture — so it isn't itself counted as a second application of this exact practice.

## Validation

- Confirm every command stated in the entry-point file actually succeeds from a clean checkout.
- Give an agent unfamiliar with the repository one small real task and confirm it can build/test using only the entry-point file, without asking for undocumented information.
pages.title: Documented repository entry points

pages.content:
# Evidence over trends

## Intent

Keep this brain's guidance grounded in observed outcomes rather than in what's popular in blog posts, vendor marketing, or a single anecdote. A practice earns a stronger status by demonstrating results, not by being repeated often.

## Rationale

Agentic-development advice moves fast and much of it is vendor-driven or untested at scale. Adopting practices because they're trending — rather than because they solved an observed problem — risks accumulating guidance that adds complexity without proven value, and that later has to be walked back. Requiring evidence at every step (see the lifecycle in ../system/governance.md) keeps the brain small and trustworthy.

## Positive signals

- Every `practice` page names the specific problem it solves and cites the observation or experiment behind it.
- A practice's `status` matches its actual evidence — `hypothesis` when untested, `experimental` while under test, `recommended`/`established` only per the promotion criteria.
- Confidence is stated qualitatively and tied to what was actually checked, not asserted.

## Negative signals

- A practice page asserts `established` status with no evidence section, or evidence that is really just "this is common advice."
- A recommendation is adopted because a specific vendor's tool supports it, rather than because it solved an observed problem.
- Confidence is stated with false numeric precision (e.g. "87% confidence") the underlying evidence can't support.

## Tradeoffs

Requiring evidence slows down adopting genuinely good ideas — a practice may sit at `hypothesis` or `experimental` for a while even when it's obviously reasonable. That's an acceptable cost: the brain optimizes for guidance the owner can trust over guidance that moves fast, and the friction is often the point of catching bad ideas before they spread.

## Related concepts

- [Verification](../concepts/verification.md) — the same "prove it, don't assume it" logic applied to code changes
- [Feedback loops](../concepts/feedback-loops.md)

## Evidence

Stated directly as a governing principle in this brain's founding spec (section 3.3); the lifecycle and promotion-criteria machinery in ../system/governance.md is the concrete mechanism that enforces it.
pages.title: Evidence over trends

pages.content:
# Progressive disclosure

## Intent

Neither this brain nor a target repository should be bulk-read by an agent. An index (or equivalent entry point) should let an agent find the few pages relevant to its current task and stop there.

## Rationale

Context windows and attention are finite and get noisier as they fill. A repository (or brain) that requires reading everything to act correctly forces agents to either skip real context or waste budget on irrelevant detail. Small, linked, well-indexed pages let an agent navigate directly to what a task needs — the same reason this brain itself is organized around `index.md` rather than one large document.

## Positive signals

- An index page exists and stays short: links and one-line descriptions, not full content.
- Pages are scoped to one topic and link out to related ones instead of repeating them.
- An agent can state which few files it needed to read to complete a task, not "I read the whole repo."

## Negative signals

- A single instructions file has grown into a multi-thousand-line document covering unrelated topics.
- Finding a rule requires searching many files with no index to narrow the search.
- New content is appended to an already-large page instead of split into a linked one.

## Tradeoffs

Splitting content into many small linked pages adds navigation overhead and risk of an agent missing a relevant page the index doesn't surface well. Mitigate by keeping the index current and requiring every new page to be reachable from it and to link at least one related page (see ../system/conventions.md's linking discipline).

## Related concepts

- [Context discovery](../concepts/context-discovery.md)
- Instruction scoping — the same principle applied specifically to how instructions are organized

## Evidence

This brain's own `index.md` was built around this principle from its first commit (see log.md, 2026-07-15 entries); the founding spec for this MVP states it explicitly as a governing rule (section 3.5).

External corroboration from a harness vendor, 2026-07-25: Anthropic moved Claude Code's code-review and verification instructions out of the always-loaded system prompt into selectively-invoked skills, and reports deleting over 80% of that system prompt with no measurable loss on internal coding evaluations — see context engineering for Claude 5 generation models. That source also records a mechanism this principle had not: disclosure can defer *tool definitions*, not only documents, with the agent searching for a tool's full schema before it becomes callable. Treat the eval claim as directional only — it is vendor-internal and not reproducible (see the reference's limits).
pages.title: Progressive disclosure

pages.content:
# Small, reversible changes

## Intent

Every improvement this brain recommends or applies to a repository should be small enough to review in one sitting and easy to undo if it doesn't help. The brain's output is "the next easiest meaningful improvement," not a large redesign.

## Rationale

Large, hard-to-reverse changes carry compounding risk: they're harder to review, harder to validate in isolation, and expensive to undo if they turn out not to help. A sequence of small, validated, reversible steps reaches the same destination with far less risk at each step, and produces a clear trail of what worked (recorded as experiments).

## Positive signals

- A proposed improvement touches a small, reviewable set of files.
- The proposal states a concrete rollback (delete the file, revert the commit) before it's applied.
- Improvements are validated independently rather than bundled with unrelated changes.

## Negative signals

- A "next improvement" proposes introducing a new system, service, or cross-cutting abstraction.
- A change can't be cleanly reverted without touching unrelated work.
- Several unrelated improvements are bundled into one proposal, making it hard to attribute outcomes.

## Tradeoffs

Small steps mean slower progress toward large structural improvements a repository might genuinely need. When a bottleneck truly requires a bigger change, say so explicitly in the assessment rather than force-fitting it into a small step — but still look for the smallest safe first move (e.g. document the problem before building the fix).

## Related concepts

- [Verification](../concepts/verification.md) — validation is what makes reversibility meaningful
- [Feedback loops](../concepts/feedback-loops.md)

## Evidence

Stated directly as a governing principle in this brain's founding spec (section 3.4); applied in ../experiments/brain/, where the first recorded experiment is deliberately scoped to one small, revertible documentation change.
pages.title: Small, reversible changes
